blocks.content: A union filesystem is the general technique of stacking several separate filesystem layers and presenting them to a process as one single, coherent filesystem. It is the concept underlying everything covered in the Image Layers topic.

Rather than storing an image as one large blob, a union filesystem keeps every layer as a genuinely separate set of files on disk, and merges them together, at read time, into what looks like a single, ordinary directory tree.

blocks.alt: Several distinct layers, stacked into one presented view

blocks.content: A process running inside a container has no idea it is actually reading from several separate layers stitched together, from its perspective, it is simply looking at one ordinary filesystem, exactly the transparency that makes containers usable at all.

blocks.alt: A seamless single filesystem, from the process's point of view

blocks.content: "Union filesystem" describes a category of techniques, not one specific piece of software, older Docker versions supported implementations like AUFS, modern Docker on Linux standardizes on OverlayFS, covered in full mechanical detail in the next topic.

Since every layer below the very top is genuinely read-only, writing to a file that already exists in one of those lower layers cannot simply modify it in place, doing so would corrupt data shared with every other image using that same layer. What actually happens instead, copy-on-write, is covered as its own topic later in this module.

blocks.alt: Writing to a read-only layer requires something more clever

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A union filesystem stacks multiple separate layers and presents them as one seamless filesystem, the general technique behind Docker's layered images.
Docker specifically uses OverlayFS today, one particular implementation of this broader union filesystem concept, covered in the next topic.
